title: Three steps of ground
hookLine: how much is enough? a small boy asks a king for three steps
tomorrow: Bali's own teacher leans in: don't give it. does Bali listen?

cards: An online cart full of things, and somehow still the feeling of not enough. The question under today's story is old: how much is enough?
Vamana walks into Bali's great sacrifice, a boy with an umbrella, and the king, known for giving, says: ask for anything. Land, cows, a village, a bride.
And the boy asks for three steps of ground, measured by his own small feet.

teach.b: Bali laughs. You're a child, he says; ask for something worth having. And Vamana answers with the line this day is built on.

Someone who isn't content with three steps, he says in the Bhagavata, won't be content even with the whole world. Wanting more never runs out; contentment is what keeps a person whole. So Bali grants the three steps.
The Sanskrit word is santosha, contentment, and in the Yoga Sutras it's one of the disciplines a person keeps: a practice, not a mood. Here's one place the neighbors say it too.
In the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, the Jewish sage Ben Zoma asks: who is rich?
And he answers: the one who is happy with his portion.
A rabbi and a young student in a Purana, landing on the same answer: enough is something you learn, not something you reach. And one honest difference.

Ben Zoma is a teacher speaking to ordinary people about their own lives. In the Purana, the one asking for so little is Vishnu himself, in disguise, and his three small steps are about to hold far more than ground.

how: In Hindu practice santosha, contentment, is counted among the disciplines of yoga, and Vamana's request is retold at festivals of Vishnu, often with the small boy holding his umbrella.

o: the ground a great sacrifice is held on
a king well-known for giving whatever he's asked
Vishnu's small form, who asked for three steps

games.q: who said enough — tap the pairs.
p: three steps, measured by his feet
ask me for anything at all
who is rich? happy with his portion

s: Vamana asks for little because he's too young to know better
he answers the king with a teaching: if three steps won't do, the world won't either.
a Jewish sage asks the same kind of question: who is rich?
Ben Zoma, in Pirkei Avot: the one who is happy with his portion.
Ben Zoma and Vamana mean exactly the same thing
a teacher's advice about your own life, and Vishnu in disguise, whose small ask will hold far more.

games.q: a yoga class lists santosha, contentment, among its disciplines. a friend says that means never wanting anything. what does Vamana's line say?
o: it's a practice of being at peace with your portion; endless wanting is what never fills.
she's right: santosha means wanting nothing at all, ever.
it's only a mood; you either feel content or you don't.
games.why: santosha is kept like a discipline. Vamana: someone not content with three steps won't be content with the world.

practice: Count, slowly, on your fingers, things already in your hands today that are enough: a meal, a person, a bed, this breath. Don't hurry to the next finger; let each one land. If you run out of fingers, start again.

wordCard.voice: Vamana: the small one, who asked a king for three steps of ground and said that if three won't do, the world won't either.

orig.note: Sanskrit: contentment. In the Yoga Sutras, one of the disciplines a person keeps.

carryVoice: For today: santosha, enough is a practice. Vamana asked a king for three steps. Day fifteen forty-six, done.
